scope: Selected primary evidence for guard diversity, partner exchanges, costs and persistence; Earth observations are not assigned as measured sky-reef traits. Access statements distinguish full accessible passages, abstracts and indexed text. No outside full papers or datasets redistributed.

sources.citation: Goheen, J. R., and Palmer, T. M. (2010). Defensive plant-ants stabilize megaherbivore-driven landscape change in an African savanna. Current Biology 20:1768–1772.
sources.access: Author-hosted full article PDF accessible; results, discussion, ant-removal and feeding-trial methods read. Supplementary material not inspected.
claims: Ant abundance negatively predicted elephant browsing after experimental ant reduction. Six elephants in feeding trials avoided ant-occupied branches when alternative forage was available.
Defense activity was assayed by counting recruited ants for 30 seconds after local thorn disturbance; this is an assay window, not a measured travel or guaranteed deterrence time.
limits: Thin skin and trunk membranes are a proposed mechanism; efficacy against arbitrary large or armored sky-reef attackers does not follow.
The four ant associates compete for exclusive host possession, so regional partner diversity is not simultaneous cooperation within each tree.

sources.citation: McKeon, C. S., and Moore, J. M. (2014). Species and size diversity in protective services offered by coral guard-crabs. PeerJ 2:e574.
sources.access: Open article PDF at marine-science repository; organism descriptions, experimental methods, results, and discussion passages inspected. Supplements not inspected; PMC browser access intermittently blocked.
claims: Pairs of 4–6 mm carapace-width crabs reduced attacks by small predatory snails; medium crabs protected against Culcita sea stars, with species-dependent efficacy; the largest tested species reduced crown-of-thorns attacks.
Across two weeks, removing the largest guard species increased attacked coral colonies from 18% to 64%, and mean tissue-volume-proxy loss from 2% to 22%.
Large colonies can contain several crab species simultaneously; small and large individuals use different parts of the branching habitat.
limits: Crab and coral size covary across experiments; no universal body-size law or biomass density can be fitted directly.
Largest-crab efficacy against smaller threats and negative interactions among all combinations were not tested. Six species appear in framing, but four were used in the stated defense experiments.

sources.citation: Youngsteadt, E., Prado, S. G., Duran Aquino, A. K., Peña Valdeiglesias, J., Gonzales Ojeda, T., and Garate Quispe, J. S. (2024). Urbanization drives partner switching and loss of mutualism in an ant–plant symbiosis. Ecology e4449.
sources.access: Publisher full-text HTML accessible; defense-assay methods, response and herbivory results, and discussion inspected. Supplementary appendix and raw data not inspected.
claims: Following local domatium flicks on Cordia nodosa, response probability was 0.88 ± 0.09 in forest plants versus 0.07 ± 0.05 in urban plants. Conditional response delays were 7.3 ± 1.6 versus 22.6 ± 5.7 seconds (model means ± SE).
Resident identity and local patrol activity changed substantially between settings; occupation of nest cavities alone did not establish protective service.
limits: This is a local emergence-and-patrol assay, with disturbance repeated after 30 seconds if needed, not successful repulsion or travel across meters of reef.
Observed urban/forest changes do not isolate one environmental cause; do not transfer these seconds to Terluna as fitted biological constants.

sources.citation: Southon, R. J., Fernandes, O. A., Nascimento, F. S., and Sumner, S. (2019). Social wasps are effective biocontrol agents of key lepidopteran crop pests. Proceedings of the Royal Society B 286:20191676.
sources.access: UCL author-accepted manuscript PDF accessible; screenhouse setup, trial methods, successful-predation results and discussion inspected. Supplements not inspected.
claims: Polistes satan captured exposed and concealed crop-pest larvae and reduced maize damage in a controlled screenhouse experiment.

Mean time to successful predation was 318 ± 56 seconds for fall armyworm and 611 ± 103 seconds for sugarcane borer; the behavioral trials lasted 45 minutes. These estimates condition on successful events.
limits: Experimental arena was 6.5 × 9.1 m, with ten provisioned colonies; this is not a measured field service radius or kilometer-scale interception response.
Supports a mobile predator guild against caterpillar-like threats, not evidence that wasps defend plants against giant attackers or recognize host emergency signals.

sources.citation: Kautz, S., Ballhorn, D. J., Kroiss, J., Pauls, S. U., Moreau, C. S., Eilmus, S., Strohm, E., and Heil, M. (2012). Host Plant Use by Competing Acacia-Ants: Mutualists Monopolize While Parasites Share Hosts. PLoS ONE 7:e37691.
sources.access: Publisher open full-text HTML; abstract, genetic/chemical design, worker-transfer methods, behavioral results, and discussion inspected. Supplementary geographic data not inspected.
claims: Integrated worker-transfer, chemical and genetic observations distinguished colony boundaries. Mutualistic Pseudomyrmex ferrugineus monopolized one or more host trees; exploitative P. gracilis could have unrelated workers sharing a host.
Workers from different host trees were often aggressive, including potentially fatal fights.
limits: Tolerance within a host does not imply service to that host; aggression between ant colonies can interrupt proposed reef-wide coordination.
Reported seconds-to-minutes concern encounters with experimentally transferred conspecific ants, not herbivore detection, so they should not parameterize guard response to grazers.

sources.citation: Palmer, T. M., Stanton, M. L., Young, T. P., Goheen, J. R., Pringle, R. M., and Karban, R. (2008). Breakdown of an ant-plant mutualism follows the loss of large herbivores from an African savanna. Science 319:192–195.
sources.access: Author/university-hosted article PDF accessible; main methods, results, and interpretation passages read. Supporting online material not inspected.
claims: Ten years of large-herbivore exclusion reduced plant housing and nectar rewards and changed ant community composition toward a poorer protector.

Ant partners had distinct conflicting incentives: some pruned growing points or destroyed nectaries; a stem-cavity associate facilitated damaging wood-borers. Longitudinal trees occupied by that associate showed about twice the mortality of trees occupied by other partners.
limits: Exclusion experimentally changed context; the eight-year mortality association is longitudinal evidence, not randomized assignment of each tree's full partner history.
Four species competing for host trees are not four species peacefully sharing every tree. Partner turnover or a territorial mosaic must be distinguished from simultaneous symbiosis.

sources.citation: Kayal, M., Ballard, J., and Adjeroud, M. (2018). Multi-species consumer jams and the fall of guarded corals to crown-of-thorns seastar outbreaks, version 2. F1000Research 6:1991.
sources.access: Open author/institution-hosted PDF; full short research note and included reviewer comments read. Supplemental image linked but not opened separately.
claims: During coral decline, investigators observed nine butterflyfish plus one crown-of-thorns simultaneously feeding on an approximately 70 cm guarded coral.
They proposed that concentration of several predator types could overwhelm guards as alternative food disappeared.
limits: Observational research note, not an experimental saturation curve; no defensible numerical guard-to-attacker threshold or independent butterflyfish contribution to mortality.
Supports testing clustered and mixed attacks, not claiming a calibrated overload mechanism for sky reefs.

sources.citation: Stanton, M. L., and Palmer, T. M. (2011). The high cost of mutualism: effects of four species of East African ant symbionts on their myrmecophyte host tree. Ecology 92:1073–1082.
sources.access: PubMed abstract and indexed first-page abstract read; attempted publisher full text and university PDF were inaccessible (publisher error/PDF 403). Not a full-paper reading.
claims: The abstract reports 4.5-year exclusion of four ant partners. Removing three Crematogaster species improved cumulative host growth and/or reproduction despite protective effects of two species.
The authors suggest rare severe elephant damage can make expensive protection valuable even when chronic-herbivory savings alone do not pay its cost.
limits: Use as an explicitly abstract-level warning about cost and time horizon; detailed methods and effect estimates need full-text access.
Reduced damage is not itself a measured positive net lifetime benefit. No quantitative maintenance cost should be transferred from this abstract.

sources.citation: Treseder, K. K., Davidson, D. W. and Ehleringer, J. R. (1995). Absorption of ant-provided carbon dioxide and nitrogen by a tropical epiphyte. Nature 375, 137–139.
sources.access: Publisher abstract and indexed excerpts of primary-paper text inspected; author repository https://escholarship.org/uc/item/2rp5h54x located. Complete scholarly reading not performed.
claims: Stable-isotope estimates attributed 39% of carbon in occupied Dischidia major leaves to ant-associated respiration and 29% of host nitrogen to ant-deposited debris.
Supports host nutrient absorption adjacent to ant nesting chambers.
limits: Particular host and isotope estimates are not transferable sky-reef fluxes.
Refixing respired carbon recycles previously fixed carbon.
Water savings from sheltered uptake should remain a hypothesis in the reef analysis, not an experimentally established reef benefit.

sources.citation: Romero, G. Q., Mazzafera, P., Vasconcellos-Neto, J. and Trivelin, P. C. O. (2006). Bromeliad-living spiders improve host plant nutrition and growth. Ecology 87, 803–808.
sources.access: PubMed abstract inspected; six-page primary PDF retrieved through UNESP and relevant text inspected. No independent reanalysis.
claims: Spiders supplied an estimated 18% of host nitrogen in a greenhouse experiment.
Plants with spiders produced leaves 15% longer in a one-year field exclusion experiment.
limits: Focal bromeliad was terrestrial; this paper alone does not establish tank-pool food-web function.
Predator waste imports nutrients only insofar as prey originated outside the host system; eating resident grazers principally recycles existing nutrients.
Percentages are Earth experimental findings, not reef parameters.

sources.citation: Ngai, J. T. and Srivastava, D. S. (2006). Predators accelerate nutrient cycling in a bromeliad ecosystem. Science 314, 963.
sources.access: PubMed abstract and indexed text of primary one-page PDF inspected; direct PDF opening failed. No supplementary-material review.
claims: Detritivores increased plant acquisition of detrital nitrogen when predatory damselfly larvae were present.
Predators reduced nitrogen export by intercepting detritivores that otherwise emerged as mobile adults.
limits: Mechanism depends on differing residence and emergence times; more predators are not universally better recyclers.
This was a nitrogen-limited bromeliad system, not demonstrated sky-reef phosphorus retention.

sources.citation: Johnson, C., Dubbs, L. L. and Piehler, M. (2023). Reframing the contribution of pelagic Sargassum epiphytic N2 fixation. PLoS ONE 18, e0289485.
sources.access: Open primary full text available; relevant methods, results and discussion inspected. Raw data not reanalysed.
claims: Twenty-four sampling occasions over six years showed strongly variable fixation, including near-zero values on several dates.
Acetylene-reduction measurements were extrapolated using an assumed mat density.
Authors observed little or no dark fixation and discuss reduced biofilm microzones protecting oxygen-sensitive nitrogenase.
limits: Provides an analogue for diazotrophs on a floating host, not an aerial fixation rate.
Nitrogen fixation supplies reactive nitrogen from N2, not phosphorus.
Hydration, phosphorus and trace-element supply, shading and day/night physiology require separate reef budgets.

sources.citation: Otero, X. L., De La Peña-Lastra, S., Pérez-Alberti, A., Ferreira, T. O. and Huerta-Diaz, M. A. (2018). Seabird colonies as important global drivers in the nitrogen and phosphorus cycles. Nature Communications 9, 246.
sources.access: Open primary full text available; relevant model description and results inspected. Population inventory and calculations not independently reproduced.
claims: Population inventory plus bioenergetics model estimated annual excretion at breeding colonies of 591 Gg N and 99 Gg P.
Concentrated seabird subsidies alter recipient habitats; trampling, salts and eutrophication also matter.
limits: The 99 Gg P value is estimated deposition at breeding colonies, not all seabird excretion everywhere.
Reef roost attendance, diet, excretion location and retention must be distinct coefficients.
Nutrient import depends on feeding outside the reef; excessive local enrichment can damage habitat.

sources.citation: Heil, M., Hilpert, A., Fiala, B. and Linsenmair, K. E. (2001). Nutrient availability and indirect (biotic) defence in a Malaysian ant-plant. Oecologia 126, 404–408.
sources.access: Primary publisher abstract inspected; full text subscription-limited. No claim of complete paper review.
claims: Nutrient supply limited Macaranga triloba food-body production.
Ant colony size correlated with host food production, and worker numbers negatively correlated with leaf damage.
limits: Does not establish a universal biomass–protection function.
Does not establish phosphorus-specific limitation in sky-reef guards.
Supports linking defender abundance to reward quality and nutrient investment, not lifting capacity alone.

sources.citation: Thornham, D. G., Smith, J. M., Grafe, T. U. and Federle, W. (2012). Setting the trap: cleaning behaviour of Camponotus schmitzi ants increases long-term capture efficiency of their pitcher plant host, Nepenthes bicalcarata. Functional Ecology 26, 11–19.
sources.access: Primary publisher full text available; relevant methods, results and discussion inspected. No independent statistical reanalysis.
claims: Ants maintained slippery pitcher rims; capture performance recovered approximately one week after experimental contamination with ants, without equivalent recovery in ant-free pitchers.
Cleaning concentrated on particular structures and was largely nocturnal.
Some removed material was deposited outside the pitcher.
limits: Demonstrates local surface maintenance, not general pathogen immunity or hull repair.
Cleaning that discards material overboard could increase reef nutrient loss.
A reef waste-transport route into recycling chambers is a proposed trait, not a result from this experiment.

sources.citation: Villamil, N., Boege, K. and Stone, G. N. (2019). Testing the Distraction Hypothesis: Do extrafloral nectaries reduce ant-pollinator conflict? Journal of Ecology. DOI 10.1111/1365-2745.13135.
sources.access: Author institutional repository abstract inspected; linked open PDF failed to retrieve and PMC opening encountered a browser challenge. Full-text review not performed.
claims: Blocking extrafloral nectar increased the fraction of flowers occupied by ants and increased fruit-abortion probability.
No detectable change occurred in numbers of ants or pollinators inside flowers.
limits: Do not describe the experiment as demonstrating reduced pollinator visitation.
Reward placement as a means to separate reef defence from reproduction is an analogue-based proposal.

sources.citation: Palmer, T. M., Doak, D. F., Stanton, M. L., Bronstein, J. L., Kiers, E. T., Young, T. P., Goheen, J. R. and Pringle, R. M. (2010). Synergy of multiple partners, including freeloaders, increases host fitness in a multispecies mutualism. PNAS 107, 17234–17239.
sources.access: Primary abstract and indexed primary full-text passages inspected; direct PMC opening encountered a browser challenge and author PDF link returned 404. Complete text and supplements not reviewed.
claims: Eight-year records of 1,750 acacias informed demographic models in which sequential sets of ant partners produced greater predicted lifetime fitness than single-partner associations.
Beneficial partner sets could include species imposing harmful short-term effects.
limits: Not evidence that all ant species coexist peacefully on one host simultaneously.
Lifetime fitness is a demographic prediction, not an experimental observation of complete century-long tree lifetimes.
Supports exploring partner succession across reef life stages rather than a universal resident mixture.
